findings.issue_text: permDenialCache entries use a different key shape (userPermDenialCacheKey) than the permission cache, so no existing invalidation path deletes them, causing stale denies to return Allowed: false for up to shortCacheTTL even after permission changes or invalidation
The deny-hit path returns before the perm-cache lookup, bypassing freshly-invalidated permission state

Denial key is built from un-resolved ParentFolder as supplied by the caller instead of the internally resolved folder tree, so the same resource's denial state may be keyed inconsistently across callers and stale denials can persist after a resource is moved or granted
permissionCacheUsage metrics are double-counted in Check: cached denials increment both a hit and a miss, systematically corrupting cache-hit rate metrics
Store errors from GetUserIdentifiers in getCachedIdentityPermissions are counted as cache misses, and the identifiers lookup is performed twice
The deny-cache hit path reuses the ('false','true') requestCount label pair for both cached allow and cached deny, losing the outcome distinction the previous full evaluation provided

New denial cache key (userPermDenialCacheKey) is not covered by existing permission invalidation logic, so stale denial entries survive permission changes until TTL expiry, incorrectly denying users who were granted access; also denial entry is set before getIdentityPermissions caches fresh permissions so the caches can disagree with no reconciliation path

Cache-key collision via unescaped underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey: distinct (userUID, action, name, parent) tuples can produce identical keys (e.g., userUID="a", action="b_c" vs userUID="a_b", action="c"), and since Name/Folder come from the request path, a crafted resource name can collide with another user's denial entry and return the wrong authorization decision

Check returns the cached deny verdict immediately without consulting the potentially fresher permission cache or singleflight path, so the highest-priority cache (denial) can be the stalest and takes absolute precedence over fresh permissions

Unbounded denial-cache cardinality: userPermDenialCacheKey embeds resource name and ParentFolder, so every denied access to a distinct resource creates a new cache entry with no size bound or eviction, allowing attacker-controlled memory growth (service.go:117, cache.go:30)

Embedded/in-process authz client caching removed: PR replaces the 30s LocalCache with NoopCache for the in-process client, so every Check/List goes to the authz service with no client-side dedup, regressing cache hit rate for embedded deployments (pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:101-104)

Missing invalidation for denial cache: permission granted after a deny may remain blocked up to shortCacheTTL because no permDenialCache invalidation is shown alongside existing permCache invalidation hooks (service.go:116-121)

getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates identifier lookup on miss path: Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions which calls GetUserIdentifiers again, and identifier store errors are silently swallowed and re-queried, doubling store load on failure paths (service.go:342-367, 126)

Metrics incorrectly labeled as cache miss: when cached perms exist but checkPermission returns allowed=false, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with "false" label even though the cache was hit, underreporting hit rate for negative-permission cases (service.go:138)

Denial-cache key instability: Check writes the denial key using the request's resolved ParentFolder, so the same dashboard resolved through different folder trees (or empty vs. resolved folder) produces different keys, causing silent cache misses for equivalent requests (service.go:117-121)

Negative (denial) cache has no invalidation path: permission-change invalidation flows cannot reconstruct the per-resource keys (_name_parent suffix), so a cached denial survives until shortCacheTTL expiry and Check returns Allowed: false after a grant, a caller-visible contract regression on the public gRPC AuthzService/Check boundary
The explicit deny entry is checked before the fresh-permission path, so even a freshly populated allow in permCache loses to a stale denial entry

ProvideAuthZClient now passes WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}) instead of the previous 30s local cache, removing all client-side response caching for the primary in-process AuthZ client path and making every authorization check a gRPC round trip, an unflagged behavioral change to public DI wiring
Denial-cache hit is reported as permissionCacheUsage WithLabelValues("true", ...), inflating the permission-cache hit metric series and masking the new cache's contribution
permissionCacheUsage metric is now emitted from List as well as user/anonymous permission fetch, changing hit/miss rate semantics on the public /metrics surface without relabeling or documentation

getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions no longer do cache-first reads (removed permCache.Get blocks); any other caller of these shared methods silently loses caching and takes a DB round trip per call

The Check fallback path after a cached-perms miss or outdated-cache result now always hits the DB even when a valid permCache entry exists for the action key, converting a cheap map miss into a full DB re-fetch

Denial cache is never invalidated on permission changes: permDenialCache entries have no Delete/invalidation path, and the new userPermDenialCacheKey format doesn't match existing invalidation targets (userPermCacheKey/anonymousPermCacheKey), so after a user is granted access Check() can keep returning Allowed: false from stale denial cache until TTL expires

Denial-cache key is ambiguous: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name, parent with '_' without escaping, allowing collisions (e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' vs name='a', parent='b_c' produce the same key) so a deny decision for one resource can be served for a different resource/parent

Denial cache key has no identity-type component, so anonymous/render service identities share denial entries with users on UID collision, and anonymous denials are stored under userPermDenialCacheKey while anonymous allow invalidation targets anonymousPermCacheKey, causing the two caches to desynchronize

Redundant GetUserIdentifiers duplicate DB work on cache-miss path: Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions which re-resolves the same identifiers, doubling ID lookups, and transient ID-store errors are silently swallowed as cache misses with no backoff, adding load to a degraded store

permDenialCache.Set result is ignored and the metrics increment at service.go:150 happens before Set could fail, making cache-write failures invisible in metrics; also denial entries written with the original request's name/parent may miss on later logically identical checks with different normalized keys (perf loss only)
No test for denial-cache invalidation: permission grants don't clear permDenialCache, allowing stale Allowed:false results for up to shortCacheTTL after a user is granted permission

Test 'Allow based on cached permissions' (~line 894) doesn't assert the DB was not consulted, so it can't distinguish a cache hit from the DB fallback path; should use a failing or call-counting fakeStore

Cache-hit test deleted from TestService_getUserPermissions (service_test.go:339-347) without replacement; no test that getUserPermissions populates the permission cache (Set side effect) after fetching from the store, and permissionCacheUsage metrics change is unverified

Denial-cache test sets permDenialCache directly instead of verifying that a denied Check populates the cache and a second Check short-circuits without hitting the DB; no coverage of the permDenialCache.Set call in service.go

No test coverage of getCachedIdentityPermissions branches: TypeAnonymous uses a different anonymousPermCacheKey, TypeRenderService always misses, and unsupported type returns an error; anonymous key-shape bugs could silently hit wrong-org data
No test that denial-cache key scoping by folder/name prevents collisions: a denial for dash1 in fold1 could deny dash1 elsewhere, or requests without a folder could collide with folder-scoped denials
Client-side RBAC caching replaced with NoopCache (rbac.go:98-103) is a behavioral change with no test or integration check confirming end-to-end caching still occurs for embedded deployments
TestService_CacheList only covers the cache-hit path; the cache-miss fallback, error path, and metric label values on each branch are untested

service.go Check (~line 116): two overlapping permission caches (permDenialCache and permCache) with no shared invalidation and unclear precedence; stale denial entries can shadow fresh allows, and correctness depends implicitly on Check's lookup ordering

service.go ~342 vs ~303: duplicated identity-type dispatch between getCachedIdentityPermissions and getIdentityPermissions (key construction, anonymous path, render-service bypass); a new identity type added in one but not the other silently bypasses caching

service.go ~347/352/359: cache.ErrNotFound leaks as a sentinel error across an internal boundary — getCachedIdentityPermissions returns store errors and cache misses in the same channel, forcing callers to compare against cache.ErrNotFound

rbac/cache.go ~30: userPermDenialCacheKey collides with userPermCacheKey's key space due to unescaped _-joined components; names/parents containing underscores can construct a denial key identical to a permission key in the shared cache instance
rbac.go ~238: NoopCache is misplaced in rbac.go instead of a cache file, uses misleading receiver name 'lc' copied from LocalCache, and hand-rolls an adapter that authzlib may already provide

service.go Check ~126–133: error-swallowing pattern `if err == nil { ... }` around cached permission check hides real store errors from GetUserIdentifiers, silently demoting genuine failures to cache misses

service.go ~137: permissionCacheUsage metric semantics silently changed — now incremented at Check/List call sites with different accounting (increments 'false' when cached perms existed but checkPermission denied, never increments on double-fetch path), breaking dashboards with no signal of the contract change

Invalidation race in pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go: a concurrent Check can write a denial entry to s.permDenialCache after invalidation runs (after a permission grant), persisting a stale negative verdict for up to shortCacheTTL (30s) that short-circuits at the top of Check and cannot be corrected except by TTL or another invalidation; the Set is not synchronized with invalidation (no singleflight or re-validation before Set)

Denial cache entries may not be covered by existing permission invalidation in pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go: userPermDenialCacheKey produces longer keys (ns.perm_uid_action_name_parent) that won't match exact-key deletes for userPermCacheKey, so denials survive invalidation entirely; no Delete/DeletePrefix call for permDenialCache is added anywhere in the PR

Unbounded cardinality/cache-pollution DoS via the denial cache: the denial key includes attacker-controlled Name and ParentFolder, so a client with valid credentials can hammer Check with distinct resource names, each a guaranteed cache miss → DB hit → denial Set, causing unbounded memory growth and guaranteed DB amplification (unlike the perm cache keyed per user/action)

ProvideAuthZClient (pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:100-105) silently drops client-side caching via NoopCache: every Check/List becomes a full gRPC round trip, behavior is inconsistent with the remote-client path which keeps its cache, and the Zanzana shadow-client path now has uncached primary plus shadow comparison traffic on every request (latency/load regression, noisier shadow metrics)

Metrics mislabeling in pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go: when getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeds (a cache hit) but checkPermission returns allowed == false, the code records permissionCacheUsage with 'false' (counting a hit-and-deny as a cache miss), undercounting hits for denial-heavy traffic

Denial cache short-circuit bypasses identity-type scoping: the denial key uses only checkReq.UserUID without identity type, so a denial for one identity type (e.g., anonymous with empty UID, or a colliding service-account UID) can short-circuit another before type-specific logic in getCachedIdentityPermissions/getIdentityPermissions is consulted

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permDenialCache entries use a different key shape (userPermDenialCacheKey) than the permission cache, so no existing invalidation path deletes them, causing stale denies to return Allowed: false for up to shortCacheTTL even after permission changes or invalidation

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a separate `permDenialCache` checked first in `Service.Check` and keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace,userUID,action,name,parent)` (includes `name` and `parent`), whereas the main permission cache uses `userPermCacheKey(namespace,uid,action)` (no `name/parent`). A cached deny will therefore persist independently of the permission map cache and will short-circuit to `Allowed: false` until `shortCacheTTL` expires (`permDenialCache.Set(...)` on deny, early return on hit). The claim that “no existing invalidation path deletes them” cannot be verified from this diff alone (no invalidation code is shown), but the key-shape divergence does create a concrete risk that any invalidation logic built around the existing permission-cache keys/prefixes would not clear denial entries, leading to stale denies for up to the TTL.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The deny-hit path returns before the perm-cache lookup, bypassing freshly-invalidated permission state

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first and on a hit returns `Allowed: false` immediately (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). This occurs before any `permCache` lookup (`getCachedIdentityPermissions`) or DB fallback (`getIdentityPermissions`). Since denial entries are written whenever `allowed` is false (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`) and there is no shown invalidation/coordination with permission changes or `permCache` invalidation, a previously-denied decision can continue to override newly-granted permissions until the denial TTL expires, producing incorrect denials.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial key is built from un-resolved ParentFolder as supplied by the caller instead of the internally resolved folder tree, so the same resource's denial state may be keyed inconsistently across callers and stale denials can persist after a resource is moved or granted

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a negative/denial cache keyed as `userPermDenialCacheKey(ns, userUID, action, name, parentFolder)` and in `Service.Check` it is built directly from `checkReq.Name` and `checkReq.ParentFolder` (see `permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)`), with no normalization/canonicalization shown in this diff. That makes the cache key dependent on the caller-provided folder context (or whatever `checkReq.ParentFolder` is derived from), which could lead to inconsistent cache hits across equivalent requests that differ only in folder representation and could leave obsolete deny entries in the cache until TTL expiry. However, the diff alone does not prove `ParentFolder` is “un-resolved” vs internally canonical, nor does it demonstrate a concrete broken authorization result, so it’s better treated as a design/edge-case concern rather than a verifiable defect from the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permissionCacheUsage metrics are double-counted in Check: cached denials increment both a hit and a miss, systematically corrupting cache-hit rate metrics

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a `permDenialCache` hit increments `permissionCacheUsage` with "true" and returns immediately, so it cannot also reach the later unconditional miss increment. For permission-map cache usage (`getCachedIdentityPermissions`), a cache hit that results in `allowed == false` only increments the "false" label (miss) and does not also increment a hit—so it may misclassify cached-deny as a miss, but it is not double-counting hits and misses for the same request as the finding claims.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Store errors from GetUserIdentifiers in getCachedIdentityPermissions are counted as cache misses, and the identifiers lookup is performed twice

adjudication.rationale: In getCachedIdentityPermissions, for user/service-account identities it calls s.GetUserIdentifiers(ctx, ns, userID) to build the cache key; on any error it returns that error. In Service.Check (and similarly List), any non-nil error from getCachedIdentityPermissions is treated as a cache miss via s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...).Inc() and then it falls back to s.getIdentityPermissions(...), which (via getUserPermissions) calls GetUserIdentifiers again. Thus: (1) identifier-store errors are counted as cache misses in the cache-usage metric, and (2) on cache-miss fallback the identifier lookup is performed twice. This is observable/perf/metrics accuracy rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The deny-cache hit path reuses the ('false','true') requestCount label pair for both cached allow and cached deny, losing the outcome distinction the previous full evaluation provided

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the `requestCount.WithLabelValues("false", "true", ...)` increment is used on the non-error path regardless of whether the permission check ultimately allows or denies (the final return after `allowed, err := ...` also always increments with ("false","true") and then returns `Allowed: allowed`). The newly added deny-cache short-circuit (`permDenialCache` hit) reuses the same label pair, but this does not remove an outcome distinction because the diff shows no prior/remaining path where `requestCount` labels differed based on allow vs deny.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New denial cache key (userPermDenialCacheKey) is not covered by existing permission invalidation logic, so stale denial entries survive permission changes until TTL expiry, incorrectly denying users who were granted access; also denial entry is set before getIdentityPermissions caches fresh permissions so the caches can disagree with no reconciliation path

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, an entry in permDenialCache is consulted first and causes an immediate deny return (service.go: new block computing permDenialKey and returning Allowed:false on cache hit). The code only ever Set()s this denial cache when a DB-backed check results in !allowed, and there is no corresponding Delete()/reconciliation when permissions later allow (no code path clears permDenialCache on success). Therefore, once a denial is cached for a (namespace,user,action,name,parent) tuple, subsequent checks will be denied until TTL expiry even if underlying permissions change to allow within that TTL. The claim about ‘not covered by existing permission invalidation logic’ isn’t verifiable from this diff, but the stale-negative-cache behavior and lack of reconciliation is directly shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cache-key collision via unescaped underscore-delimited concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey: distinct (userUID, action, name, parent) tuples can produce identical keys (e.g., userUID="a", action="b_c" vs userUID="a_b", action="c"), and since Name/Folder come from the request path, a crafted resource name can collide with another user's denial entry and return the wrong authorization decision

Check returns the cached deny verdict immediately without consulting the potentially fresher permission cache or singleflight path, so the highest-priority cache (denial) can be the stalest and takes absolute precedence over fresh permissions

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new denial cache is consulted first and returns an immediate deny (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`) before checking `permCache` (via `getCachedIdentityPermissions`) or falling back to `getIdentityPermissions`/singleflight. Because `permDenialCache` entries are written on any DB-based deny (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`) and have a TTL, a previously denied decision will continue to hard-deny even if permissions have since changed to allow within that TTL. This matches the finding: the denial cache takes absolute precedence and can be staler than the permission cache/DB path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unbounded denial-cache cardinality: userPermDenialCacheKey embeds resource name and ParentFolder, so every denied access to a distinct resource creates a new cache entry with no size bound or eviction, allowing attacker-controlled memory growth (service.go:117, cache.go:30)

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `permDenialCache` and populates it on every denied `Check` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`), where `permDenialKey` is constructed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` and thus varies with attacker-controlled `Name` and `ParentFolder` (service.go:113-151, cache.go:30-32). The underlying cache shown in tests is `cache.NewLocalCache` configured only with time-based expiry/cleanup and no max-size bound, so a client can generate many distinct denial keys within the TTL window and cause unbounded in-memory growth until expiry.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Embedded/in-process authz client caching removed: PR replaces the 30s LocalCache with NoopCache for the in-process client, so every Check/List goes to the authz service with no client-side dedup, regressing cache hit rate for embedded deployments (pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:101-104)

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the in-process/embedded client created in `ProvideAuthZClient` was changed from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` to `authzlib.NewClient(..., authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)` (rbac.go around the shown hunk). `NoopCache.Get` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`, so this client will never serve responses from a client-side cache. Meanwhile the remote client path still uses `cache.NewLocalCache` with a 30s expiry. This is a real, diff-grounded performance/behavioral change (reduced client-side caching) but not a correctness defect proven by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing invalidation for denial cache: permission granted after a deny may remain blocked up to shortCacheTTL because no permDenialCache invalidation is shown alongside existing permCache invalidation hooks (service.go:116-121)

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `permDenialCache` and in `Service.Check` it is consulted first: if the denial key is present it immediately returns `Allowed: false` without checking cached perms or falling back to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB) (service.go: added block using `permDenialCache.Get` before any permission fetch). The denial entry is set whenever a DB-backed check returns `!allowed` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`). There is no mechanism shown in the diff to clear that denial entry when permissions change, so a previously denied resource will remain denied until `shortCacheTTL` expires even if the underlying permissions are granted shortly after. This is a correctness regression because it can return false negatives and, unlike the positive-perms cache path, there is no fallback revalidation when the cached deny is hit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getCachedIdentityPermissions duplicates identifier lookup on miss path: Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions which calls GetUserIdentifiers again, and identifier store errors are silently swallowed and re-queried, doubling store load on failure paths (service.go:342-367, 126)

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` is called and its error is ignored unless `err == nil` (new logic around `service.go` Check). For user/service-account identities, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` before checking `permCache` and returns `cache.ErrNotFound` on a cache miss. Check then falls through to `getIdentityPermissions(...)`, which (via `getUserPermissions`) performs another `GetUserIdentifiers(...)` lookup. This duplicates identifier-store work on the common miss path, and also swallows identifier lookup errors (no logging/return) and immediately retries the same lookup in the DB path, potentially doubling load/latency on failure paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Metrics incorrectly labeled as cache miss: when cached perms exist but checkPermission returns allowed=false, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with "false" label even though the cache was hit, underreporting hit rate for negative-permission cases (service.go:138)

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, when cached permissions are found (err == nil) but checkPermission returns allowed == false, the code does not increment permissionCacheUsage with label "true" and then unconditionally increments it with "false" after the cache attempt (before the DB fetch). This means a cache hit that still requires fallback is counted as a "false" usage (service.go: new block around the cachedPerms/checkPermission logic). This is a real, diff-grounded metrics semantics issue, but it only affects observability (hit-rate reporting), not authorization correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial-cache key instability: Check writes the denial key using the request's resolved ParentFolder, so the same dashboard resolved through different folder trees (or empty vs. resolved folder) produces different keys, causing silent cache misses for equivalent requests (service.go:117-121)

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the denial-cache key is computed from `checkReq.ParentFolder` (service.go) and includes it in `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)`. However, the finding’s core claim—that `ParentFolder` is a “resolved” value that can vary for equivalent requests (e.g., different folder trees or empty vs resolved), causing *silent misses for equivalent checks*—is not verifiable from the diff because the construction/normalization of `checkReq.ParentFolder` is not shown. From the diff alone, different `ParentFolder` values producing different keys is expected behavior, not demonstrably an instability/defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Negative (denial) cache has no invalidation path: permission-change invalidation flows cannot reconstruct the per-resource keys (_name_parent suffix), so a cached denial survives until shortCacheTTL expiry and Check returns Allowed: false after a grant, a caller-visible contract regression on the public gRPC AuthzService/Check boundary

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new negative cache (permDenialCache) keyed by namespace/user/action/name/parent (userPermDenialCacheKey) and makes Check short-circuit to `Allowed: false` on any cache hit before consulting permission data (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). The denial entry is written on any DB-derived denial (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true) }`). Within the shown changes there is no corresponding invalidation/delete of these per-resource denial keys when permissions are later granted, so a stale deny can persist until shortCacheTTL and incorrectly deny despite an updated allow state.

matched_golden_ids: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same core problem: the permission cache contains a deny/false entry for the scope, so `checkPermission` will treat it as not allowed even if the test/comment expects cached permissions to “allow access.” The candidate frames it as deny taking precedence over an allow path, which explains why the false cache entry blocks access.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ProvideAuthZClient now passes WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}) instead of the previous 30s local cache, removing all client-side response caching for the primary in-process AuthZ client path and making every authorization check a gRPC round trip, an unflagged behavioral change to public DI wiring

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ProvideAuthZClient` replacing `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` with `authzlib.NewClient(channel, authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, and `NoopCache.Get` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`. That removes the previous local-cache behavior for the in-process client wiring path (while `newRemoteRBACClient` still uses `cache.NewLocalCache` with 30s expiry). This is a concrete, diff-grounded behavioral/performance change in DI wiring, but not a correctness defect per se.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial-cache hit is reported as permissionCacheUsage WithLabelValues("true", ...), inflating the permission-cache hit metric series and masking the new cache's contribution

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a hit in the new `permDenialCache` path increments `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action)` (see the early-return block after computing `permDenialKey`). That metric label/value is also used for regular permission-cache hits, so denial-cache hits will be counted as permission-cache hits, inflating that series and obscuring the denial cache’s separate impact. This is a real, diff-grounded observability/metrics attribution issue, not a functional correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permissionCacheUsage metric is now emitted from List as well as user/anonymous permission fetch, changing hit/miss rate semantics on the public /metrics surface without relabeling or documentation

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves `permissionCacheUsage` emissions away from the permission-fetch functions and into request handlers: cache hit/miss increments were removed from `getUserPermissions` (and `getAnonymousPermissions` no longer checks cache directly), while `Service.Check` and `Service.List` now call `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and emit `permissionCacheUsage` based on that result. `Check` also increments `permissionCacheUsage` on an explicit denial-cache hit. This changes what the metric represents (request-level cache usage including denial short-circuit and List-path usage) versus previously mostly fetch-level cache usage, which can change hit/miss rates on `/metrics` without any relabeling or documentation in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions no longer do cache-first reads (removed permCache.Get blocks); any other caller of these shared methods silently loses caching and takes a DB round trip per call

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove cache-first reads inside the shared helpers: in `getUserPermissions` the `s.permCache.Get(...)` fast path and related metrics increments were deleted, and in `getAnonymousPermissions` the `s.permCache.Get(...)` fast path was also deleted. Caching is now done by the new `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)`, which `Check` and `List` call before falling back to `getIdentityPermissions(...)`. However, the diff does not show whether any other code path calls `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` directly (or calls `getIdentityPermissions` without the new cache-first wrapper). If such callers exist, they would now always hit the store via `singleflight` instead of returning cached values, which is a real perf/behavioral change but not a correctness bug proven by this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The Check fallback path after a cached-perms miss or outdated-cache result now always hits the DB even when a valid permCache entry exists for the action key, converting a cheap map miss into a full DB re-fetch

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, if `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns a cached perms map but `checkPermission` evaluates to `allowed == false`, the code falls back to `s.getIdentityPermissions(...)` (DB/store path). After this diff, `getIdentityPermissions` no longer re-checks `permCache` because the cache lookups were removed from `getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions` (see deletions around `userPermKey := ...` and `anonPermKey := ...`). Therefore, the fallback always performs a store/DB fetch even though a valid `permCache` entry for the action key exists—turning a cached negative into a DB hit (at least once, until `permDenialCache` is populated). This is a performance/behavior tradeoff rather than a correctness defect, since it avoids false-denies due to stale/partial caches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache is never invalidated on permission changes: permDenialCache entries have no Delete/invalidation path, and the new userPermDenialCacheKey format doesn't match existing invalidation targets (userPermCacheKey/anonymousPermCacheKey), so after a user is granted access Check() can keep returning Allowed: false from stale denial cache until TTL expires

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `permDenialCache` and makes it authoritative in `Service.Check()`: if `s.permDenialCache.Get(...)` hits, `Check()` immediately returns `Allowed: false` without falling back to DB (`service.go` new early-return block). The cache entry is set whenever a DB-backed check is denied (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`). In this diff there is no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation path for `permDenialCache` entries, so a permission change (deny -> allow) can be masked by a stale denial until `shortCacheTTL` expires. This stale-deny risk is specific to the new denial cache because the normal permission cache path *does* fall back to DB when cached permissions don’t allow, but the denial cache prevents that fallback.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial-cache key is ambiguous: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name, parent with '_' without escaping, allowing collisions (e.g. name='a_b', parent='c' vs name='a', parent='b_c' produce the same key) so a deny decision for one resource can be served for a different resource/parent
matched_golden_ids: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same underlying issue: `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds the cache key by concatenating components with underscores without escaping or handling empty/underscore-containing parts, which can cause ambiguous keys/collisions and lead to incorrect denial cache hits affecting permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache key has no identity-type component, so anonymous/render service identities share denial entries with users on UID collision, and anonymous denials are stored under userPermDenialCacheKey while anonymous allow invalidation targets anonymousPermCacheKey, causing the two caches to desynchronize

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the denial cache is consulted/stored using `permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` and `userPermDenialCacheKey` is built only from `namespace + userUID + action + name + parent` (no `IdentityType`). That makes denial entries potentially shared across different identity types that may use the same `UserUID` string (e.g., user vs service-account vs render-service), which can incorrectly deny access for a different principal. The second claim about anonymous-specific cache invalidation/desynchronization isn’t directly shown in the diff (no invalidation logic here), but the identity-type omission in the denial key is a concrete, diff-grounded correctness issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Redundant GetUserIdentifiers duplicate DB work on cache-miss path: Check falls through to getIdentityPermissions which re-resolves the same identifiers, doubling ID lookups, and transient ID-store errors are silently swallowed as cache misses with no backoff, adding load to a degraded store

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows a new cache-fast-path in `Service.Check`: it calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)`, which for `TypeUser`/`TypeServiceAccount` calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` to build the permission cache key. On any non-nil error it falls through to `getIdentityPermissions(...)`, which (via `getUserPermissions`) will resolve `GetUserIdentifiers` again, duplicating identifier resolution on the cache-miss/outdated-cache path. Also, `Check` ignores/logs nothing about errors from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` (it only acts when `err == nil`), so transient identifier-store errors can be treated like a cache miss and immediately retried via the slower path, adding load and potentially masking the original error source. This is a performance/observability issue grounded in the diff, not a correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: permDenialCache.Set result is ignored and the metrics increment at service.go:150 happens before Set could fail, making cache-write failures invisible in metrics; also denial entries written with the original request's name/parent may miss on later logically identical checks with different normalized keys (perf loss only)

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the metrics increment shown in the diff (`requestCount...Inc()`) occurs after the `permDenialCache.Set(...)` call, not before it, so the claim about ordering is not supported by the change. Also, from the diff we cannot verify that `permDenialCache.Set` returns an error/result that is being ignored—`cacheWrap.Set`’s signature/behavior isn’t shown and test usage suggests it may not return anything. The point about denial keys missing due to different “normalized” keys is speculative: the diff doesn’t show any normalization logic or evidence that logically identical checks would use different `Name/ParentFolder` values.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test for denial-cache invalidation: permission grants don't clear permDenialCache, allowing stale Allowed:false results for up to shortCacheTTL after a user is granted permission

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, a permDenialCache hit short-circuits and immediately returns Allowed:false without consulting cached perms or the DB (service.go: new block using permDenialKey and s.permDenialCache.Get). The code also sets permDenialCache on any computed denial (if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }) but never clears it on later allows. This makes a previously denied (name,parent) check potentially stay denied until shortCacheTTL even if the underlying permissions in the store change to allow, unlike the positive-permissions cache path which falls back to DB when cached perms don't allow. The diff adds tests for denial-cache presence but none covering this stale-deny/invalidation behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test 'Allow based on cached permissions' (~line 894) doesn't assert the DB was not consulted, so it can't distinguish a cache hit from the DB fallback path; should use a failing or call-counting fakeStore

adjudication.rationale: In `TestService_CacheCheck` subtest "Allow based on cached permissions", the test preloads `s.idCache` and `s.permCache` and only asserts `resp.Allowed` is `true`. It does not set `s.store`/`s.permissionStore` to a failing or call-counting fake, nor does it assert those stores were not invoked. From the diff, nothing in this test would definitively prove the code path used cached permissions rather than falling back to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB/store) if the implementation changed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cache-hit test deleted from TestService_getUserPermissions (service_test.go:339-347) without replacement; no test that getUserPermissions populates the permission cache (Set side effect) after fetching from the store, and permissionCacheUsage metrics change is unverified

adjudication.rationale: The cache-hit test in `TestService_getUserPermissions` is removed (service_test.go around the shown deletion), and the new tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only validate behavior when the cache is pre-populated and that `Check/List` fall back to DB on cache miss/outdated cache. They do not assert that a store-backed call results in `permCache.Set(...)` (i.e., cache population as a side effect) nor do they verify `permissionCacheUsage` metric increments, which were moved to `Check`/`List` (service.go: cache-hit/miss accounting around `getCachedIdentityPermissions`). This is a specific coverage gap introduced by the refactor, not a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial-cache test sets permDenialCache directly instead of verifying that a denied Check populates the cache and a second Check short-circuits without hitting the DB; no coverage of the permDenialCache.Set call in service.go

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, new logic populates `permDenialCache` when a DB-backed permission check returns `!allowed` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`), and future calls short-circuit early if that key is present. The added test `TestService_CacheCheck/"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry"` sets `s.permDenialCache` directly and only validates the early-return path, but it does not exercise/verify that an initial denied `Check` call causes the cache entry to be written and that a second `Check` avoids hitting the store. Thus the new `permDenialCache.Set` behavior is currently not covered by tests in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test coverage of getCachedIdentityPermissions branches: TypeAnonymous uses a different anonymousPermCacheKey, TypeRenderService always misses, and unsupported type returns an error; anonymous key-shape bugs could silently hit wrong-org data

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new branching logic in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` for `TypeAnonymous`, `TypeRenderService`, and a default error path (`unsupported identity type`) in `pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go`, but the added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only exercise the `TypeUser`/`TypeServiceAccount` path via `Subject: "user:test-uid"`. There is no test coverage verifying the anonymous cache-key path (`anonymousPermCacheKey(ns.Value, action)`), the intentional always-miss behavior for `TypeRenderService`, or the error returned for unsupported identity types. The note about key-shape bugs causing wrong-org hits is speculative from the diff alone, but the lack of branch coverage for these newly added code paths is a concrete, diff-grounded review issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test that denial-cache key scoping by folder/name prevents collisions: a denial for dash1 in fold1 could deny dash1 elsewhere, or requests without a folder could collide with folder-scoped denials

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new denial cache keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` and uses it in `Service.Check` (`permDenialKey := ...checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder`). A new test only covers the positive deny case (`Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`) but does not assert non-collision behavior (e.g., that a deny for `name=dash1,parent=fold1` does *not* deny `dash1` in a different folder or a request with empty/no folder). Since this is newly introduced cache-key scoping logic, the missing test is a concrete, diff-grounded review issue, but not a provable defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client-side RBAC caching replaced with NoopCache (rbac.go:98-103) is a behavioral change with no test or integration check confirming end-to-end caching still occurs for embedded deployments

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows an explicit behavioral change for embedded/in-process usage: ProvideAuthZClient now constructs the authz client with `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})`, whereas the remote client path still uses a real `cache.NewLocalCache(...)`. That means client-side caching is disabled specifically for the embedded client. The added tests exercise server-side cache behavior in `Service.Check`/`Service.List`, but there is no end-to-end or integration-style check covering the embedded deployment path (client -> in-process gRPC server) to ensure caching expectations/performance behavior remain acceptable. This is a concrete, diff-grounded coverage concern rather than a proven correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: TestService_CacheList only covers the cache-hit path; the cache-miss fallback, error path, and metric label values on each branch are untested

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the newly added TestService_CacheList only sets idCache/permCache and verifies List returns items on a cache hit. It does not exercise the new cache-miss fallback branch in Service.List (the `else` that calls `s.getIdentityPermissions(...)` after `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error), nor any error propagation from that fallback. Also, no tests in the added code assert `permissionCacheUsage` metric label values that are now incremented differently on hit vs miss (`WithLabelValues("true"|"false", listReq.Action)`), so those branches’ metric behavior is unverified here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: service.go Check (~line 116): two overlapping permission caches (permDenialCache and permCache) with no shared invalidation and unclear precedence; stale denial entries can shadow fresh allows, and correctness depends implicitly on Check's lookup ordering

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `permDenialCache` that is consulted first in `Service.Check` and returns `Allowed: false` immediately if the key exists (service.go: `if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). That denial entry is set after a DB-backed check returns `allowed == false` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`). There is no logic shown to clear/invalidate that per-resource denial when permissions later become allowed (e.g., after role/permission changes), and because the deny short-circuits before both `permCache` evaluation and the DB call, a stale denial will incorrectly override a fresh allow until the denial TTL expires. This is a correctness bug introduced by the new precedence/negative-cache behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: service.go ~342 vs ~303: duplicated identity-type dispatch between getCachedIdentityPermissions and getIdentityPermissions (key construction, anonymous path, render-service bypass); a new identity type added in one but not the other silently bypasses caching

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new helper `getCachedIdentityPermissions` with its own `switch idType` dispatch (Anonymous => cache key, RenderService => bypass, User/ServiceAccount => identifiers+key, default error). The main permission path still exists separately in `getIdentityPermissions` (not shown fully here), meaning identity-type handling is now split across two functions. This duplication is real and diff-grounded: future additions/changes to supported identity types could be implemented in one function but not the other, leading to inconsistent caching behavior (e.g., silently no-cache or different errors). This is a maintainability/consistency risk rather than a currently verifiable functional defect introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: service.go ~347/352/359: cache.ErrNotFound leaks as a sentinel error across an internal boundary — getCachedIdentityPermissions returns store errors and cache misses in the same channel, forcing callers to compare against cache.ErrNotFound

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` does return `cache.ErrNotFound` on cache misses, but callers (`Service.Check` and `Service.List`) do not compare against `cache.ErrNotFound` (or any sentinel). They only branch on `err == nil` vs `err != nil` and treat any non-nil error as a cache miss/fallback path. Therefore the claim that this “forces callers to compare against cache.ErrNotFound” is not supported by the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: rbac/cache.go ~30: userPermDenialCacheKey collides with userPermCacheKey's key space due to unescaped _-joined components; names/parents containing underscores can construct a denial key identical to a permission key in the shared cache instance

adjudication.rationale: In rbac/cache.go the new userPermDenialCacheKey builds keys by concatenating variable components with '_' (namespace+".perm_"+userUID+"_"+action+"_"+name+"_"+parent) and uses the same ".perm_" prefix as userPermCacheKey. With no escaping/length-prefixing, different (action,name,parent) tuples can produce the same string (e.g., name="a_b", parent="c" collides with name="a", parent="b_c"), which can cause incorrect cache hits/denies. Because both caches share the same underlying cache instance (service.go constructs permCache and permDenialCache from the same cache), any cross-key collision also risks type/value confusion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: rbac.go ~238: NoopCache is misplaced in rbac.go instead of a cache file, uses misleading receiver name 'lc' copied from LocalCache, and hand-rolls an adapter that authzlib may already provide

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add a `NoopCache` type at the end of `rbac.go`, but the criticism that it is "misplaced" and the receiver name `lc` being "misleading" are subjective style/organization nits rather than a verifiable defect or concrete review issue. Also, the claim that this adapter is redundant because `authzlib` "may already provide" one cannot be confirmed from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: service.go Check ~126–133: error-swallowing pattern `if err == nil { ... }` around cached permission check hides real store errors from GetUserIdentifiers, silently demoting genuine failures to cache misses

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, errors from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` are not returned immediately (only `err == nil` is handled), but they are not “silently demoted to cache misses” in a way that hides real store errors: for the user/service-account path, `getCachedIdentityPermissions`’s only non-cache error source is `GetUserIdentifiers`, and `Check` then unconditionally calls `getIdentityPermissions`, which (via `getUserPermissions`) calls `GetUserIdentifiers` again and will propagate the error if it persists. Thus genuine store failures are not hidden by this pattern; at most it causes an extra attempt / delayed surfacing and potentially skewed cache-hit metrics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: service.go ~137: permissionCacheUsage metric semantics silently changed — now incremented at Check/List call sites with different accounting (increments 'false' when cached perms existed but checkPermission denied, never increments on double-fetch path), breaking dashboards with no signal of the contract change

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves `permissionCacheUsage` accounting out of the cache lookup functions and into `Check`/`List`. In `Check`, even when cached permissions are found (`getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns `err == nil`), the metric is only incremented with `("true", action)` on the *allowed* early-return path; if cached perms exist but `checkPermission` returns `allowed == false`, the code falls through and unconditionally increments `permissionCacheUsage` with `("false", action)` (treating a cache hit as a miss). Also, the perm-denial cache early return increments `permissionCacheUsage` with `("true", action)` even though that path is not a permission-cache hit. This is a real, diff-grounded semantic change that can affect monitoring/dashboards, but it’s not a functional correctness defect in authz behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Invalidation race in pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go: a concurrent Check can write a denial entry to s.permDenialCache after invalidation runs (after a permission grant), persisting a stale negative verdict for up to shortCacheTTL (30s) that short-circuits at the top of Check and cannot be corrected except by TTL or another invalidation; the Set is not synchronized with invalidation (no singleflight or re-validation before Set)

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `permDenialCache` that is checked at the very start of `Service.Check` and immediately returns `Allowed: false` on a cache hit (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false} }`). Later, when a DB-backed evaluation yields `!allowed`, it unconditionally writes `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`. There is no re-validation before writing the denial entry and no mechanism shown here to clear/override this negative cache on subsequent permission grants, so a prior deny can incorrectly short-circuit and keep denying until TTL expiry. The finding’s mention of an “invalidation race” specifically isn’t shown in this diff, but the core stale-negative behavior is directly introduced by the new denial cache short-circuit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache entries may not be covered by existing permission invalidation in pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go: userPermDenialCacheKey produces longer keys (ns.perm_uid_action_name_parent) that won't match exact-key deletes for userPermCacheKey, so denials survive invalidation entirely; no Delete/DeletePrefix call for permDenialCache is added anywhere in the PR

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `permDenialCache` (Service fields/init) and writes to it in `Service.Check` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`) and reads it early (`Get(...)`), but the PR does not add any corresponding invalidation/cleanup path for these denial entries (no `permDenialCache.Delete(...)` or similar appears in the shown changes). The specific claim about “existing invalidation in pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go” and exact-key deletes cannot be verified from this diff (cache.go here only defines key helpers), but it is verifiable that a new cache dimension (`userPermDenialCacheKey` includes name/parent) is added without any explicit invalidation hooks beyond TTL, which could leave stale denials until expiry if the system relies on explicit cache invalidation elsewhere.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unbounded cardinality/cache-pollution DoS via the denial cache: the denial key includes attacker-controlled Name and ParentFolder, so a client with valid credentials can hammer Check with distinct resource names, each a guaranteed cache miss → DB hit → denial Set, causing unbounded memory growth and guaranteed DB amplification (unlike the perm cache keyed per user/action)

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `permDenialCache` keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` (see `cache.go`) and used in `Service.Check` to short-circuit denies (`permDenialCache.Get` early return) and to record denies (`permDenialCache.Set` when `!allowed`). Because `name` and `parent` come directly from the request (`checkReq.Name`, `checkReq.ParentFolder`), a caller can generate arbitrarily many distinct cache keys by varying these fields, causing unbounded cache growth (until TTL/cleanup) and repeated DB work on each novel key (cache miss -> `getIdentityPermissions(...)` DB path -> denial Set). The underlying cache shown in tests is `cache.NewLocalCache` with only time-based expiry and no size bound, so this is a verifiable cache-pollution/DoS risk introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ProvideAuthZClient (pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:100-105) silently drops client-side caching via NoopCache: every Check/List becomes a full gRPC round trip, behavior is inconsistent with the remote-client path which keeps its cache, and the Zanzana shadow-client path now has uncached primary plus shadow comparison traffic on every request (latency/load regression, noisier shadow metrics)

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ProvideAuthZClient switched from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` to `authzlib.NewClient(channel, authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, and `NoopCache` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound` on `Get`, effectively disabling client-side caching on this path. In contrast, `newRemoteRBACClient` now constructs an authz client with `cache.NewLocalCache(...)`, so caching remains enabled for remote clients. Also, when `featuremgmt.FlagZanzana` is enabled, `zanzana.WithShadowClient(rbacClient, zanzanaClient, reg)` will use this uncached primary client, plausibly increasing per-request traffic/latency and affecting shadow comparisons. This is a diff-grounded performance/consistency concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Metrics mislabeling in pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go: when getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeds (a cache hit) but checkPermission returns allowed == false, the code records permissionCacheUsage with 'false' (counting a hit-and-deny as a cache miss), undercounting hits for denial-heavy traffic

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, a cache hit is only counted as a hit when it results in an early return on `allowed == true` (it does `permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", ...)` inside that branch). If `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeds but `checkPermission` returns `allowed == false`, control falls through to `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()` (the unconditional increment after the cache attempt), recording it as a cache miss. This mislabels hit-and-deny cases in the metric, but it does not change authorization behavior—only observability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Denial cache short-circuit bypasses identity-type scoping: the denial key uses only checkReq.UserUID without identity type, so a denial for one identity type (e.g., anonymous with empty UID, or a colliding service-account UID) can short-circuit another before type-specific logic in getCachedIdentityPermissions/getIdentityPermissions is consulted

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, the new denial-cache short-circuit runs before any identity-type-specific permission logic and builds permDenialKey via userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, ...), omitting checkReq.IdentityType. That means the denial cache is keyed only by namespace+userUID+action+name+parentFolder, so a denial entry can apply across different identity types that share the same UserUID value (and it bypasses getCachedIdentityPermissions/getIdentityPermissions which do scope by IdentityType). This is a correctness/security risk inherent in the key design shown in the diff.
